label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
claim: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
quote: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
scope: human perception and methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis
measurable_quantities: accuracy with which simple-program models reproduce human perceptual judgments
algorithmic size of standard analysis procedures
candidate_data: Published psychophysics and visual-neuroscience datasets on feature detection, together with open-source implementations of standard compression and statistical procedures.

label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
claim: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
quote: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.
scope: inference of generating rules from the output of cellular automata and other simple programs
measurable_quantities: success rate of rule-inference or program-synthesis methods given only final patterns
computational cost of identifying the generating rule
candidate_data: Patterns generated with public cellular automaton software (e.g. Wolfram Language or Golly) used as benchmarks for existing program-synthesis and system-identification methods.

label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
claim: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
quote: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.
scope: definitions of randomness, including description-length (algorithmic) definitions
candidate_data: none known

label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
claim: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
quote: something should be considered to be random whenever there is essentially no simple program that can succeed in detecting regularities in it.
scope: the definition of randomness for data of any kind
candidate_data: none known

label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
claim: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
quote: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.
scope: detection of regularities in sequences and images by simple programs
measurable_quantities: fraction of data sets passing a few standard tests that are later failed by other tests
agreement between independent randomness tests
candidate_data: Public randomness test batteries such as the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite, TestU01 and Dieharder applied to many sequences.

label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
claim: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
quote: when we say that something seems complex, what we are effectively saying is that our powers of perception and analysis have failed on it.
scope: the definition of complexity
candidate_data: none known

label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
claim: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
quote: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.
scope: human visual attention and aesthetic preference for images
measurable_quantities: aesthetic ratings or viewing/fixation times versus compressibility of global and local image features
candidate_data: Published eye-tracking and image aesthetic-rating datasets (e.g. AVA aesthetic visual analysis dataset), combined with compression-based complexity measures.

label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
claim: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
quote: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.
scope: lossless data compression algorithms applied to patterns from simple programs
measurable_quantities: compression ratios of standard compressors on uniform, repetitive, nested and complex cellular automaton patterns
candidate_data: Standard open-source compressors (gzip, bzip2, xz/LZMA, zstd) applied to cellular automaton patterns generated with public software.

label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
claim: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
quote: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.
scope: lossy transform-based image compression of simple, random and complex images
measurable_quantities: fraction of transform coefficients needed for feature recognition
perceptual quality versus compression rate by image class
candidate_data: Public image collections (e.g. Kodak image set, USC-SIPI image database) and open JPEG/Walsh–Hadamard transform implementations, together with perceptual-quality measures.

label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
claim: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
quote: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.
scope: human visual texture perception
measurable_quantities: texture discrimination performance versus differences in local 2×2 block statistics at equal overall density
candidate_data: Published psychophysical texture-discrimination studies and texture image databases (e.g. Brodatz textures), plus primary visual cortex receptive-field recordings.

label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
claim: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
quote: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.
scope: human visual recognition of repetitive and nested two-dimensional patterns
measurable_quantities: accuracy of human observers classifying patterns as repetitive, nested or random
candidate_data: Psychophysics experiments using patterns from two-dimensional substitution systems generated with public software.

label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
claim: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
quote: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.
scope: human auditory perception of sounds generated from discrete sequences
measurable_quantities: listener discrimination of nested versus random sequence sonifications
number of spectral peaks at which tones are no longer heard
candidate_data: Auditory psychophysics experiments using sonified substitution-system sequences; existing literature on pitch perception and auditory masking.

label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claim: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
quote: In most cases, the typical behavior produced by the model looks considerably more random than the data.
scope: statistical modeling of data generated by deterministic simple programs
measurable_quantities: discrepancies in higher-order statistics and visible structure between data and samples from fitted models
candidate_data: Cellular automaton data generated with public software and fitted with standard statistical packages for Markov and hidden Markov models.

label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
claim: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
quote: it has sometimes been thought that if one could just compute frequencies of blocks of all lengths one would have a kind of universal test for randomness. But sequences like (e) and (f) on the facing page make it clear that this is not the case.
scope: block-frequency tests for randomness of binary sequences
measurable_quantities: block frequencies and their variance for LFSR and Champernowne-type binary sequences versus random sequences
candidate_data: Sequences computable with standard tools; the binary Champernowne sequence is catalogued in the OEIS.

label: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
claim: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.
quote: statistical analysis, even with some generalization, cannot readily recognize that sequences like (g) and (h) are anything but completely random—even though at an underlying level these sequences were generated by quite simple rules.
scope: the rule 30 center-column sequence and the binary expansion of pi
measurable_quantities: p-values from standard randomness test batteries
block-frequency deviations relative to random sequences
candidate_data: Rule 30 center column (catalogued in the OEIS) and published high-precision digits of pi, tested with NIST SP 800-22, TestU01 or Dieharder.

label: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
claim: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.
quote: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.
scope: stream ciphers based on cellular automata, specifically rule 30
measurable_quantities: computational cost of key recovery from known keystream for rule 30 ciphers versus established ciphers
candidate_data: Published cryptanalysis literature on cellular automaton stream ciphers and standard cryptographic test suites.

label: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
claim: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.
quote: it is my guess that in the end it will in fact turn out to be possible to get a formula for any nested pattern in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions
scope: nested patterns generated by substitution systems
measurable_quantities: existence of closed-form hypergeometric expressions for cell colors of specific nested patterns
candidate_data: Computer algebra systems and the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions for hypergeometric identities.

label: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
claim: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simple mathematical formula.
quote: So even if one allows rather general structure, the evidence is that in the end there is no way to set up any simple formula that will describe the outcome of evolution for a system like rule 30.
scope: formula representations of cellular automaton evolution, especially rule 30
measurable_quantities: number of terms in minimal DNF expressions per step
minimal Nand circuit size per step
candidate_data: Boolean minimization tools (e.g. Espresso logic minimizer) and SAT-based exact circuit synthesis applied to rule 30.

label: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
claim: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.
quote: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.
scope: mechanisms of human memory storage and retrieval
measurable_quantities: invariance of neural population responses to small input changes
similarity-based recall performance
candidate_data: Neurophysiological recordings of sensory and hippocampal neurons (e.g. Allen Brain Observatory) and work on locality-sensitive hashing in olfactory circuits.

label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
claim: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
quote: My strong suspicion is that the use of memory is what in fact underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking.
scope: human cognition
measurable_quantities: dependence of reasoning performance on familiarity with argument patterns
speed of memory retrieval versus stepwise reasoning
candidate_data: Published cognitive psychology studies of content effects in reasoning (e.g. Wason selection task) and analogical retrieval.

label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
claim: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
quote: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.
scope: human thinking and its emulation by artificial systems
measurable_quantities: size of the simplest systems that emulate general human-like thinking
candidate_data: none known

label: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
claim: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.
quote: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.
scope: artificial intelligence and emulation of human thinking
candidate_data: none known

label: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting
claim: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in perception.
quote: Most of them, for example, recognize repetition, and some also recognize nesting. But almost none recognize anything more complex.
scope: human perception and standard methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis
measurable_quantities: performance of standard analysis methods on repetitive, nested and more complex generated data
candidate_data: Standard compressors and statistical test suites applied to benchmark sets of patterns generated by simple programs.

label: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
claim: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.
quote: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.
scope: all possible methods of perception and analysis
candidate_data: none known

label: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages
claim: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.
quote: it seems far from inconceivable that some of the extraterrestrial radio and other signals that we pick up and assume to be random noise could in fact be meaningful messages
scope: astronomical radio and other signals searched for extraterrestrial intelligence
measurable_quantities: compressibility or detectable algorithmic structure in signals classified as noise
candidate_data: Breakthrough Listen open data archive of radio observations.
